## Roadmap

Date: 2026-09-30. This section turns the design above (sections 1 to 20), the pamoja template extraction (research-pamoja-template.md) and the salvage map (salvage-map.md) into an ordered plan. It adds no new architecture; where it names a mechanism, the design section that owns it is cited in parentheses. Owner decisions taken after that date are written in where they apply, each with its date: the release 1 benchmark method and the go decision (R.2; R.3 rows 7 and 14; R.7 item 1), the httparse exception (R.2; R.3 row 3), the conformance test-name rule (R.2), the single-version policy (R.1 item 4; R.3 rows 14, 22 and 34; R.7 item 12) and the sdk publish under `next` (R.7 item 4). Text they replace is either rewritten or kept and marked as history. R.3 rows 1 and 9 were corrected on 2026-10-02 to where the probe reruns live and to the release 1 WebSocket and SSE count.

12. The local rules file for the new repository (ignored machine-wide, never committed; content mirrors pamoja's conventions, read, plus the zero-server engineering rules from its local rules file):

    ```
    # zero-core (zero-server native core)

    One memory-safe Rust core for the zero-server product, exposed to TypeScript (Node),
    Python and C# through idiomatic bindings. MIT licensed. Remote: https://github.com/molexxxx/zero-core

    ## Stack and layout
    - Cargo workspace at the repository root; capability crates under `crates/` (one
      responsibility per crate, named `zero-<capability>`); the bundle crate is `crates/zero-server`;
      the C ABI is `crates/zero-ffi` (cbindgen header `include/zero.h`, regenerated on every build).
    - `bindings/node` (napi-rs, `@zero-server/*`), `bindings/python` (PyO3 plus hatchling,
      `zero-server-*`), `bindings/dotnet` (`[LibraryImport]`, `ZeroServer.*`): standalone crates
      and projects excluded from the workspace, built by their own pipelines.
    - `conformance/vectors.json` is generated by `cargo run -p zero-examples --example conformance_vectors`
      and asserted by all three bindings; `conformance/api-surface.json` is the export contract.
    - `docs/standards.toml` is the conformance registry (migrated from zero-server's
      docs/STANDARDS.md); `docs/capabilities.toml` claims every library crate exactly once;
      `docs/lints/*.toml` are the three lint tables `cargo xtask lints --check` enforces.
    - `crates/xtask` is the task runner (`cargo xtask <task>`); `crates/zero-bench` holds the
      TechEmpower entries and the measurement gates and is never published.

    ## Commands
    - Build: `cargo build --workspace`; test: `cargo test --workspace`; no_std: `just nostd`
    - Lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; format check: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
    - Everything CI runs: `just ci`; task list: `cargo xtask`
    - Bench: `just bench <entry>` (Linux host or container; see docs/about/benchmarking.md)

    The local toolchain is scoop-based and has no rustfmt, clippy or rustup. Verify behavior
    locally with `cargo build` and `cargo test`; run rustfmt and clippy in Docker before every
    commit that touches Rust (the `rust:latest` image does not ship the components; the
    `zero-core-lint` image built from `.docker/lint.Dockerfile` adds them):
    - `docker build -t zero-core-lint -f .docker/lint.Dockerfile .docker` (once, and after pulling rust:latest)
    - `docker run --rm -e CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/t -v "C:/Users/tonyw/Desktop/projects/zero-core:/work" -w /work zero-core-lint cargo fmt --all`
    - `docker run --rm -e CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/t -v "C:/Users/tonyw/Desktop/projects/zero-core:/work" -w /work zero-core-lint bash -c "cargo fmt --all -- --check && cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings"`
    Do not hand-guess rustfmt output: it rewraps at fn_call_width (about 60 columns), not only at
    max_width. A crate is immutable once on crates.io, so the fmt and clippy job must be green
    before any publish.

    ## Engineering rules (strict)
    ### Standards-first
    - Every feature maps to a row in `docs/standards.toml` (RFCs at rfc-editor.org, W3C and WHATWG
      specs, protobuf.dev, the gRPC PROTOCOL-HTTP2 document, Prometheus exposition format, W3C Trace
      Context, NIST SP 800-63B, OWASP cheat sheets, the vendor reference for each database dialect).
    - Before implementing, changing or reviewing any protocol, wire format, parser, header, cookie,
      crypto or auth behavior: fetch the cited source live, read the section, and work from that
      text. Never implement standards behavior from memory. No row: add one first and fetch it.
    - Cite the source in code (`@see <url>#section` in the rustdoc of the item that implements it)
      and in the commit body. Conformance tests are named after the statement they check and carry
      the section number; every row carries a `release` field and `cargo xtask standards --check`
      enforces the rows at or below the current release.
    - Only the current document counts (RFC 9110 to 9112 not 2616 or 7230 to 7235; RFC 9113 not
      7540; RFC 8489 not 5389; RFC 8656 not 5766). Update the row when a source is obsoleted.
    - Security defaults follow the standard's MUST and SHOULD plus the referenced BCP (RFC 8725 for
      JWT, RFC 9700 for OAuth 2.0, rfc6265bis for cookies). Deviations require a rationale in the
      rustdoc and a test that pins the behavior.

    ### Dependencies and unsafe
    - Zero third-party crates in every crate that neither terminates TLS, hosts QUIC, sits on the
      runtime seam, makes raw OS calls, wraps the C library nor crosses a language boundary. The
      others carry the pinned allowlist in `deny.toml`; any crate not listed is denied.
    - `unsafe_code = "forbid"` everywhere except the audited crates (zero-simd, zero-server-crypto,
      zero-ffi, zero-sys, zero-sqlite, zero-plugin, bindings/node, bindings/python/packages/native),
      which use `deny` with per-item allows and a `// SAFETY:` comment on every block.
    - no_std crates carry `#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]`, `extern crate alloc`, the
      no_std lint table (no indexing, unwrap, expect, panic or unchecked arithmetic), and build
      with `--no-default-features` on the host and for thumbv7em-none-eabihf in CI.
    - Installing any binding never compiles anything: prebuilt binaries for the seven targets in
      the release workflows; native code is never a build-time requirement of a user.

    ### Testing
    - No fixed sleeps to wait for an assertion: poll, use fake time, or await the real event.
      Every bug fix ships with a test that fails on the previous code.
    - Parsers of untrusted input carry proptest tests and a libFuzzer target and never panic on
      arbitrary bytes. Tests anchor to the specification's own vectors, not to round-trips alone.
    - `Cargo.lock` is committed in the workspace and in every binding; `npm ci` and `cargo vet`
      must pass from the committed lockfiles. Linux-only failures are reproduced in a container
      before code changes.

    ### Conventions
    - American English everywhere (color, behavior, license, catalog, serialize, analyze, artifact,
      canceled, judgment, while). Regular dashes only; no em or en dashes; no horizontal rules.
    - Rustdoc with `# Arguments`, `# Returns`, `# Errors` on every public item; `missing_docs` is
      denied; crate READMEs, `include/zero.h`, `index.d.ts`, `__init__.pyi` and
      `conformance/vectors.json` are generated: edit the source and regenerate, never the artifact.
    - Comments sparse; module headers and public-item docs only; no inline narration.
    - No planning vocabulary in code, docs or commits (no iteration labels, no numbered plan
      references). Describe the change and its reason in professional engineering terms.
    - Examples and guides build values with library calls; never paste byte blobs.
    - Every change that ships or removes a capability audits `web/home.toml`, the README and the
      capability and standards pages in the same commit.
    - Planning markdown lives in `.docs/` (gitignored). Commits: short imperative subject, authored
      as molexxxx, no AI attribution, nothing referencing the assistant reaches the remote.
    ```

13. Before the first tag: probe every unprobed `zero-<capability>` crate name and apply the `zero-server-<capability>` rule on collision (section 18 question 11); create the nuget.org trusted-publishing policies for `ZeroServer`, `ZeroServer.Core` and `ZeroServer.Native` and the PyPI projects `zero-server`, `zero-server-native` and `zero-server-core` (section 3); run `cargo xtask release --plan` and `--dry-run`.

### R.2 First deliverable: the thesis proof

Definition. An HTTP/1.1 server built from the release 1 crates that exist at that point (`zero-core`, `zero-limits`, `zero-simd`, `zero-http-types`, `zero-date`, `zero-http1`, `zero-router`, `zero-uri`, `zero-qs`, `zero-mime`, `zero-base64`, `zero-json`, `zero-sys`, `zero-io` on `io-tokio`, `zero-rt` with tier 0 and tier 4 dispatch, `zero-http`), driven by the two `zero-bench` entries of section 12.5 (`zero-server`, Realistic, the entry that goes through the router with the `zero-limits` defaults (owner decision 2026-10-02; the earlier text added the `zero-policy` defaults); `zero-server-plt`, Stripped and Platform) and a thin `zero-serve` main, with no binding, no TLS and no host language on any path. It proves the design's thesis in its narrowest form: an in-house reject-not-normalize parser with SIMD scans, prebuilt response blocks, a per-core arena with no global allocation per request and one worker per core (section 1 goal 1, section 6.2, 6.3, 5.6) beats Drogon on json as a Realistic entry, and it does so before any of the binding, TLS, HTTP/2, database or HTTP/3 work exists, so a miss is found at day 84 rather than day 203.

Conformance content. The registry's HTTP conformance statements are the 27 statements under "HTTP semantics, routing, and responses" and the 13 under "HTTP/1.1 message framing" (read from `docs/STANDARDS.md`, lines 34 to 60 and 70 to 82; 40 in all), plus the rows section 12.1 adds for the section 6.2 rules (RFC 9112 sections 2.2, 3.2.2, 6.1 and 6.3; RFC 9110 sections 5.5, 6.5.1 and 8.6) and the `responseSplitting` vectors of section 6.3. Each becomes one `#[test]` or one `http1Parser` or `router` vector named after the statement, with the section number in the name or in the registry row's URL fragment and note (owner decision 2026-10-02; `RULES.md`, Standards-first); `xtask standards --check` is green for every row whose `release` is 1 in those two sections; the `zero-http1` fuzz targets have run for at least 24 CPU-hours on the request and trailer parsers with no crash, and so has the `httparse` differential target on the request head parser (the duration is a starting value, judgment). httparse is admitted for that target alone by the owner's fuzz-only exception to the 12-month currency rule (2026-10-02; `RULES.md`, Currency): its newest stable release is 1.10.1, created 2025-03-03 (crates.io, fetched 2026-10-02), and the crate does not declare itself finished, so it is a dependency of `fuzz/` only, as the differential oracle of the HTTP/1.1 head parser, and never enters a shipped graph. The 16 "Static files and conditional requests" statements and the "WebSocket and server-sent events" statements (33 read; 27 are release 1 rows since the registry moved `realtime-19` to `realtime-23`, permessage-deflate, to release 3 and `realtime-24`, WebSocket over HTTP/2, to release 2) belong to steps 9 and later, not to this deliverable.

Measurement and acceptance for release 1 (owner decision 2026-10-02, which replaces the rented tiers and the ratio gates kept below as history):

- Method: release 1 is benchmarked in Docker on the owner's Ryzen 9 9950X3D desktop under WSL2, the server and the load generator on separate cpusets and the fuzz container paused, by the method of `RULES.md` (Conventions): the median of five interleaved runs, the ratio against each entry measured in the same session beside every absolute number, every error counter at zero, and the raw data with the command that reproduces it committed under `bench/results/<date>/`.
- Entries: the Realistic `zero-server` entry (through the router with the `zero-limits` defaults) and the Platform entry `zero-server-plt`, beside the language groups of the owner's decision of 2026-10-01: Rust (hyper, axum and actix-web, with Drogon as the C++ reference) and Node (node:http, Express, Fastify and uWebSockets.js), each group with its two zero-server rows (routes answered in Rust, and a handler written in that language), every entry built and configured the way its own project documents for production.
- Waived for release 1: the rented tier A and tier C runs, and with them tier B, which runs on the tier A host's link.
- No ratio gates release 1: every ratio is published as measured, whatever it is, with the hardware stated as one desktop under WSL2.
- Gates recorded on the same runs (section 5.7): the counting allocator asserts zero global-allocator calls per request on the plaintext and json routes of the Realistic entry through accept, parse, route, policy, handler, serialize and writev; bytes per idle connection at 10k, 100k and 1M connections on `io-tokio` with the lazy-lease policy; the 16,384-connection plaintext level with zero errors; the cost of `overflow-checks = true` measured by one run with it off (informational; the shipped profile keeps it on unless section 18 question 12 is invoked for `zero-simd`); the 16-connection json figure recorded beside the entries that escape the 25K to 30K band.

Pass rule (owner decision 2026-10-02). The deliverable passes when the allocator gate holds and the five-run session is committed under `bench/results/<date>/` with zero errors in every published cell; no ratio, against Drogon or any other entry, is a condition of this deliverable or of the release 1 tag. Go decision: the owner's go decision is this decision, dated 2026-10-02 (none was recorded before step 8, where the stop rule below placed it).

The original measurement plan, kept as history; its margins remain the section 13 targets and gate nothing at release 1 (section 12.5 procedure; section 13 rows; every reference number is Round 23 on Round 23 hardware and the self-run publishes ratios on its own hardware):

- json, tier A (one rented Linux host or two instances on one switch, the pinned Round 23 Drogon entry rebuilt from the archived tree at commit 523534bb beside the two entries): the Realistic `zero-server` entry at a ratio of at least 1.10 over Drogon (Drogon's Round 23 figure is 2,474,350, so 1.10 corresponds to 2.72M on that hardware; the expected band is 2.72M to 2.9M, carried), zero errors at 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512 connections, five interleaved runs, medians compared, the ratio above 1.10 in every run. The `nodejs` and `uwebsockets.js` entries from the same tree run in the same session and their numbers are recorded, not gated.
- plaintext, tier B (whatever link the tier A host has): the ratio of each entry against the ceiling reference (libreactor, with faf second; section 18 question 14) at 256, 1,024, 4,096 and 16,384 connections, zero errors at every level; no Drogon plaintext ratio is published from this tier because a 10 GbE or slower link caps every entry alike (section 12.5).
- plaintext, tier C (rented bare metal with a 25 or 40 GbE link between load generator and server, one run before the release 1 tag): the Realistic entry at least 1.10 over Drogon at the best level and at 16,384 connections with zero errors, and parity (at least 1.00) with zero errors at 256 connections (section 13 rows 1 to 3; the Realistic tokio precedents that meet these are hyper and xitca-web, carried). The Platform entry is reported against the ceiling reference only.

Pass rule and stop rule of the original plan, kept as history: Pass rule. The deliverable passes when the tier A json ratio, the tier B plaintext ceiling ratio and the allocator gate hold; the tier C run is a precondition of the release 1 tag, not of this deliverable, because it depends on rented hardware (section 16 hardware line, 4 days). Stop rule. If the json ratio is below 1.00 after the section 13 levers have been measured one at a time (buffer-direct JSON writer, prebuilt blocks, per-core Date, one writev per burst, no per-request allocation), the owner decides whether to continue before step 8 starts; the design carries no fallback that changes this number by more than the tokio-against-compio spread (section 13, cross-cutting), so the decision is about the thesis, not about the driver.

Effort: 84 engineer-days (range 70 to 100; judgment), which is steps 1 to 7 of R.3 and a subset of the 203-day release 1 figure of section 16.

### R.4 The HTTP/3 step (step 23) in full

Deliverable. `zero-quic` behind the `http3` cargo feature: one quinn-proto endpoint per core over the datagram batch seam (`quinn-proto` with `default-features = false, features = ["rustls-aws-lc-rs"]`), the connection ID allocator encoding the core index, connection-id handoff over the seam's wake as the default steering path, the opt-in `SK_REUSEPORT` eBPF program with its raw `bpf(2)` loader in `zero-sys` and its privileged-runner test, the 0-RTT policy layer (off by default; 425 per RFC 8470 when enabled), qlog hooks; the h3 adapter in `zero-http` mapping `zero-h3` frames and `zero-qpack` field sections onto the same `RequestHead` and `ResponseHead` the h1 and h2 paths produce (section 6.1), with `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` 32,768 and the section 10.4 QUIC limits; `rustls::quic::ServerConnection` over the same resolver, ticketer and staple with `h3` added to the ALPN list on the QUIC listener only; compiled into every published binary, runtime-off (`listen({ http3: false })`), Windows functional only as section 6.5 states; `zero doctor` reporting UDP reachability, steering mode and the DNS line `HTTPS 1 . alpn="h3,h2"` (section 6.5; whether that record shape is what RFC 9460 prescribes is unverified here, since RFC 9114 section 3 does not mention DNS records at all per the fetch in this task).

Alt-Svc advertisement. RFC 9114 section 3.1.1 (fetched) states that an origin "can advertise the availability of an equivalent HTTP/3 endpoint via the Alt-Svc HTTP response header field or the HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame using the 'h3' ALPN token", with the example `Alt-Svc: h3=":50781"`, and section 3.2 that "HTTP/3 support is indicated by selecting the ALPN token 'h3' in the TLS handshake". RFC 7838 section 3 (fetched) gives the grammar `Alt-Svc = clear / 1#alt-value`, `alt-value = alternative *( OWS ";" OWS parameter )`, `alternative = protocol-id "=" alt-authority`, `alt-authority = quoted-string`, `parameter = token "=" ( token / quoted-string )`; section 3.1 states that an advertised alternative "is considered fresh for 24 hours from generation of the message" and that "A field value containing the special value 'clear' indicates that the origin requests all alternatives for that origin to be invalidated"; section 2.1 requires that "Clients MUST have reasonable assurances that the alternative service is under control of and valid for the whole origin"; and section 3.1 describes `persist=1` as a hint that the service "is potentially useful beyond a network configuration change". The step therefore emits `Alt-Svc: h3=":<udp-port>"; ma=86400` on h1 and h2 responses only while a QUIC listener is bound with the same certificate and the operator has set `http3.advertise = true` or `http3.probe_from`, never with a different host and never with `persist=1`; emits `Alt-Svc: clear` for one `ma` period after HTTP/3 is disabled; and emits nothing by default (section 6.5, section 18 question 17). The HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame is not emitted in this step (the header reaches h2 clients as an ordinary response field; the frame is an open question, R.7 item 13).

Conformance vectors added by this step, all generated by the examples crate and asserted by the three runners: `altSvc` (rendered header for advertise on, off, after disable within `ma`, after `ma` expiry, with a non-matching certificate, and the `persist` parameter absent in every case), `h3Settings` (the SETTINGS frame bytes for capacity 0, blocked streams 0 and field section size 32,768, and the rejection of a peer SETTINGS that omits a required default), `earlyData` (425 with `Early-Data: 1` on a non-safe route, acceptance on a route flagged `early_data`, deferral until handshake completion otherwise), `quicLimits` (stream and data limits from section 10.4 as transport parameters), plus the existing `qpack` and `h3Frames` sections extended with the RFC 9114 section 7 frame types the adapter now handles. Registry rows added with `release = 3`: RFC 9000, 9001, 9002, 9114, 9204, 7838 and 8470 (section 12.1), each with `anchor = "vector"` or `"interop"`.

Exit criteria. `cargo test --workspace --features http3` green on Linux, macOS and Windows; the default graph carries no quinn, tracing or quic crate (`cargo tree` diff in CI) and `deny/http3.toml` is accepted by the owner (section 18 question 3); the quic-interop-runner cases handshake, transfer, retry, resumption, ecn, keyupdate and http3 pass against quic-go and ngtcp2 as registered in the runner's Docker set; the headless Chrome and Firefox check loads a page over h1, receives Alt-Svc, and the harness asserts the second load used h3; a NAT-rebinding test exercises the connection-id handoff; the h1 Realistic entry's json and plaintext ratios are unchanged within the run-to-run noise of section 12.5 with `http3` compiled in and runtime-off; a CPU-per-request measurement of the QUIC path with GSO, GRO and ack frequency is recorded (the Fastly parity band is a promotion criterion, section 6.5, not an exit criterion of this step). Promotion to default-on is a later owner decision (section 18 question 10). Effort 25 days (18 core, 5 eBPF loader and test, 2 browser check; section 16).

### R.5 The zero-server transition

The Node repository at `C:\Users\tonyw\Desktop\projects\zero-server` keeps publishing `@zero-server/sdk` (1.1.0 today, measured) until the parity gate. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (fetched) requires a MAJOR increment for "any backward incompatible changes", a MINOR increment for "new, backward compatible functionality", a PATCH increment for "backward compatible bug fixes", and states that before functionality is removed in a major "there should be at least one minor release that contains the deprecation so that users can smoothly transition". The Node.js release schedule (fetched) has Node 20 at end-of-life since 2026-04-30, Node 22 in Maintenance LTS until 2027-04-30, Node 24 as Active LTS until 2028-04-30 and Node 26 as Current with end-of-life 2029-04-30, each LTS line supported 30 months. The `npm deprecate <package-spec> <message>` command (fetched) "will update the npm registry entry for a package, providing a deprecation warning to all who attempt to install it", accepts a range such as `"< 0.2.3"`, and is reversed with an empty message; the reference does not describe any effect on existing installs beyond that warning.

Maintenance releases that still ship from the Node repository:

- 1.1.1 (PATCH, security): the section 15.3 list (the audit's critical and high fixes already in the working tree plus the remaining ones from salvage-map.md section 3), the NPM_TOKEN renewal and the release-on-bump fix so a tag publishes under `latest` rather than `alpha`. Ships before step 1 starts, because its users are the ones the transition must keep. No engine change (dropping Node 20 from `engines` would be an incompatible change under the semver text above). Effort about 8 days (new, judgment).
- 1.2.0 (MINOR, correctness and types): the section 15.3 list (transactions, audit and tenancy on every adapter, the Model and CLI fixes, the HTTP and gRPC correctness list, `types/index.d.ts` compiling with `skipLibCheck=false`, removal of the "documented but not implemented" claims). It is also the deprecation release the semver text calls for: every item of the section 15.2 drop list that is reachable from the public surface (`clusterize` and `ClusterManager` as features, `memoryCheck`, `eventLoopCheck`, `diskSpaceCheck`, the JSON file adapter, `PluginManager`, `DatabaseView`, `Query.cache()`, `res.push()` and the static `push` option, the WebRTC media adapters, recording, ingress, cascade, the E2EE helpers, `Fake`, `Factory`, `Seeder`, `SeederRunner` as core features) emits one runtime deprecation warning per process on first use naming the 2.0.0 replacement or the removal, and the CHANGELOG lists each with its reason. Node 20 leaves the CI matrix (it is end-of-life per the fetched schedule) while the `engines` field stays unchanged in 1.x. Ships during release 1 (before step 14), so that it is the last 1.x feature release and no user waits on it. Effort about 20 days (new, judgment).
- 1.2.x: security patches only, from the Node repository, for as long as the support window below runs.

When `@zero-server/sdk` becomes the binding:

- From step 13 (release 1): `@zero-server/sdk@2.0.0-alpha.N` published from `zero-core/bindings/node` under the dist-tag `next`, exact-pinned on `@zero-server/native@2.0.0-alpha.N` and `@zero-server/core@2.0.0-alpha.N`, so early users can run tiers 0, 3 and 4 with the release 1 caveats of section 4.4 (buffered bodies only, no TLS options beyond the release 1 set, no database). `latest` stays on 1.x.
- From step 22 (release 2): `2.0.0-beta.N` under `next` with HTTP/2, streaming bodies, PostgreSQL and tier 2, the Python and .NET facades published as their own pre-releases.
- At step 34 (parity gate): `2.0.0` under `latest`. The package name, the `createApp` surface, the error classes, the Model classes, `clusterize` as a shim and the `env` loader keep their shapes (section 15.3); the section 15.2 drop list is the documented breaking change set in the 2.0.0 CHANGELOG. The 14 existing scoped packages are handled by name: a name that survives as a facade (section 15.3 names `@zero-server/core` and one facade per capability) is republished at 2.0.0 from `zero-core`; a name that does not survive is deprecated at 2.0.0 with `npm deprecate "@zero-server/<name>@*" "<message naming the replacement>"`. From 2.0.0 the Node repository publishes nothing new; its `main` receives a final commit pointing at `zero-core` and the repository is archived after the 1.x support window.

How the vitest corpus becomes the acceptance suite (section 12.3 classification; 128 files and 7,685 cases measured in this task):

- Step 13 copies `zero-server/test/` into `zero-core/bindings/node/test/legacy/` with the scripted rewrite of relative `require` paths onto `test/_shim/` (vitest's alias does not redirect CommonJS `require`, carried), and `test/_helpers.js` unchanged. A `legacy-manifest.json` maps every file to `{ release: 1 | 2 | 3, status: "run" | "skip" | "dropped", reason }`: the 724 facade-only cases in the ten HTTP suites are `run` at release 1 where their feature exists (app, routing, realtime, errors, env), `skip` with the release that ships their feature otherwise; the 2,659 cases that use the Node http objects are `skip` until step 32 ships the emulation and then `run` at release 3; the ORM (2,319), adapter (861), WebRTC (528) and docs (532) suites are assigned in steps 25, 24, 29 and 33; the 21 coverage-only files and the adapter-internals files are `dropped` with a section 12.3 reason.
- CI runs every `run` entry whose release is at or below the current release and fails on any failure; a `skip` entry whose release is at or below the current release fails the build, so a feature cannot ship without its suite. Legacy tests are never hand-edited: when one fails because a behavior changed deliberately, the change is a 2.0.0 CHANGELOG entry and the test moves to `dropped` with the CHANGELOG anchor as its reason; when it fails for any other reason, the binding is wrong. The parity gate (step 34) requires zero `skip` entries and every `dropped` entry to cite a section 15.2 item or a CHANGELOG anchor.
- The documentation example runner (`test/docs/manifest-validation.test.js`) transfers with the docs data format and runs the guides' Node examples (section 12.3).

Deprecation policy from 2.0.0 onward (proposed; owner decision R.7 item 11): the four published surfaces (npm, PyPI, NuGet, crates.io) share one version from one tag; a facade's major is the only version a user tracks, because each facade exact-pins its native package; deprecations are announced in a MINOR with a runtime warning on first use, a CHANGELOG entry and a doc note, and removed no earlier than the next MAJOR, per the semver text above; the C ABI is additive within a major (`ZERO_ABI_VERSION` in the header increments only on a removal or a signature change, and `zero_plugin_abi_version` is checked before `zero_plugin_register`, section 10.8); the previous major receives security patches for 12 months after the next major's general availability, and the 1.x line follows the same rule counted from the 2.0.0 date; `npm deprecate "@zero-server/sdk@<2.0.0" "<message>"` runs at the end of that window, not at 2.0.0, so 1.x users are not warned while their line is still supported.

### R.7 Open questions with recommended defaults

The section 18 questions stand; these are the ones this roadmap adds.

1. Tier C timing. Decided 2026-10-02 (owner): the rented tier A and tier C runs are waived for release 1; release 1 is measured in Docker on the owner's Ryzen 9 9950X3D desktop under WSL2 by the R.2 method, no ratio gates the release, and the ratios are published as measured. The earlier default, kept as history: run the rented 25 or 40 GbE plaintext measurement once, before the release 1 tag (step 14), and accept the first deliverable on tier A and tier B alone. Default: yes; the json ratio and the ceiling ratio are the thesis, and the tier C run buys the plaintext-against-Drogon number the design promises without blocking 84 days of work on hardware rental.
2. `rust-version` pin. Default: `1.89` as pamoja pins (read), raised only when a crate needs a newer stable feature, with the MSRV job as the proof; the local cargo 1.96.0 and the container's 1.98.0 (measured) both exceed it.
3. Node 20 in the 1.x CI matrix. Default: removed from CI in 1.2.0 because the line is end-of-life (fetched schedule), `engines` left unchanged in 1.x so the change is not a semver-incompatible one; 2.0.0 sets `engines.node` to `>=22` (the napi CLI itself requires Node 20.17, 22.13 or 23.5 and later, carried from salvage-map.md).
4. When the `next` dist-tag opens. Default: at the release 1 tag (step 14), as `2.0.0-alpha.1`, with the release 1 caveats stated in the package README; not earlier, because a pre-release without TLS or WebSocket ABI would be judged against 1.1.0. Decided 2026-10-02 (owner): yes; `@zero-server/sdk` publishes `2.0.0-alpha.1` under `next` together with `@zero-server/core` and `@zero-server/native`, which replaces any text that kept the sdk private until parity.
5. Order of 1.2.0 against release 1. Default: 1.2.0 ships before the release 1 tag, because it is the deprecation release the semver text requires and its fixes are owed to current users regardless of the core.
6. The 1.x security window. Default: 12 months after 2.0.0 general availability, then `npm deprecate` on the `<2.0.0` range and archive of the Node repository.
7. .NET target framework. Default: `net8.0` as pamoja (read), with `net10.0` added to the dotnet.yml matrix; the section 2 probes ran on .NET 10.0.2 and whether any `[LibraryImport]` or `[SuppressGCTransition]` behavior differs on net8.0 is unverified.
8. Where the first deliverable's server lives. Default: the two `zero-bench` entries, with `zero-serve` as a thin main over the same crates, so the number is measured on the product path and not on a demo binary.
9. The plugin loader's 8 days. Default: kept as a release 3 line (step 31), since section 10.8 makes the trust model a precondition of shipping the crate and section 16 did not price it.
10. Legacy suite location and manifest. Default: `bindings/node/test/legacy/` with `legacy-manifest.json` as R.5 describes; the alternative (rewriting the suites into the facade's own test tree) discards the measured salvage value.
11. Deprecation policy text. Default: the R.5 policy (announce in a MINOR, remove no earlier than the next MAJOR, 12 months of security patches for the previous major, additive C ABI within a major).
12. Crate versions against package versions. Decided by the owner (2026-10-01, confirmed 2026-10-02): the single-version policy. The crates and every package share one version, published to crates.io, npm, PyPI and NuGet from one tag: `2.0.0-alpha.1` at release 1 (PyPI spells it `2.0.0a1`; npm publishes pre-releases under `next`), then `2.0.0-beta.N`, then `2.0.0` at the parity gate. `xtask version` keeps one version site, as pamoja does, and the C ABI's compatibility is carried by `ZERO_ABI_VERSION` (R.5), not by the crate version. The superseded default, kept as history: crates stay 0.x (0.1.0 at release 1, 0.2.0 at release 2, 0.3.0 at parity) while the facades go 2.0.0-alpha, 2.0.0-beta and 2.0.0, because the C ABI and the Rust API are not frozen at parity; `xtask version` therefore carries two version sites (crate and package) rather than pamoja's one, which is a change to the copied `version.rs` and to `release-preflight.yml`. The alternative, one shared version, is what pamoja does and is simpler; it would put the crates at 2.0.0 with a pre-1.0 ABI.
13. The HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame (RFC 9114 section 3.1.1 names it as the second advertisement path; fetched). Default: not emitted in step 23; the response header reaches h2 clients as an ordinary field; revisit if the browser check shows an h2 client that ignores the header.
14. Fuzz duration before a codec ships. Default: 24 CPU-hours per target on the weekly job with the crash corpus committed, as the exit criteria above use; the number is a starting value with no fetched basis.
15. Docker lint image. Default: the `.docker/lint.Dockerfile` image (`zero-core-lint`) rebuilt on each `rust:latest` pull, because the measured `rust:latest` on this host ships neither component and the one-off command downloads them on every run.

The application's workarounds are framework requirements. Each one below is fixed in the core or the facade in the step named, and R.8 is complete only when the rebuilt application contains none of them:

1. Listing moved to `/list` because a child mount dropped the path with a query string; fixed in zero-server 1.1.0 and carried by the router semantics transfer (step 6).
2. The SSR catch-all lives on a child router mounted last because an app-level `GET /*` hid mounted routers; the router defines mount precedence over wildcards (step 6) and the facade documents it.
3. `sync()` never alters an existing table, so the application runs raw `ALTER TABLE` and rebuilds tables to relax `NOT NULL`; `zero-orm` migrations and snapshot diff (step 25).
4. Composite unique keys and secondary indexes cannot be expressed in the schema DSL and are created with raw DDL; the schema model gains both (step 25).
5. Custom audit events go through the private `audit._writeEntry`; the audit write path gets a public `record` call (step 24, the audit write path is per driver).
6. `TYPES.JSON` returns a raw string from SQLite and five readers parse it by hand; the `Value` model decodes JSON columns in the driver (step 24).
7. `deleteWhere` supports equality only, so rows are deleted one at a time or with raw SQL; `deleteWhere` and `updateWhere` accept the query builder's predicates (step 25).
8. An atomic conditional increment is raw SQL; `updateWhere` accepts expression values (step 25).
9. The SDK `fetch` sends no `User-Agent`; `zero-fetch` sends `zero-server/<version>` by default (step 19).
10. `canJoin` and `verifyClient` are synchronous, so membership checks run a synchronous raw SQLite query and the WebSocket guard cannot load a user; both hooks are batched host calls that can await (step 9 for WebSocket accept, step 29 for rooms).
11. The mesh peer cap only emits an event; the core enforces it and the facade exposes the limit (step 29).
12. `peerMessageRate` default of 30 is too low for this application; the default is reviewed against this workload (step 29).
13. The signaling hub is not a `WebSocketPool`, so a duck-typed adapter exists; the realtime pool and the signaling hub share one room model (step 29).
14. The env url validator keeps a trailing slash, breaking WebAuthn origins; `zero-env` normalizes (step 22).
15. Helmet's CSP is off because a per-request nonce is needed; the security-headers rule supports a nonce placeholder filled per request on tier 0 (step 9).
16. `res.raw` and `req.raw` are used for every streamed byte, `req.user` is overwritten by a ticket guard, the `_dt` cookie hash is reimplemented, and `trustedDevice.issue` is wrapped in a Promise to call it directly; the streaming ABI (step 16), a documented request-local slot, a public device fingerprint function and non-middleware auth entry points (step 26) remove every `raw` access.

Deliverables of R.8:

- The application on `@zero-server/sdk` 2.0.0 with every route working, zero `res.raw`, `req.raw` or `adapter._db` access, the sixteen items above closed, and `@zero-transfer/sdk` kept for storage (out of scope for the core).
- Resumable upload of a 1 GiB object in 512 MiB windows through the streaming ABI with the checkpoint store, download with byte ranges, and a streamed folder bundle, each measured against the current Node version of the application on the same host with requests per second, bytes per second and resident memory published as ratios beside the absolutes.
- Chat over the WebSocket ABI and mesh signaling over `zero-webrtc` with the existing zero-query frontend unchanged.
- A test suite for the application (it has none today): route tests through the facade's test helpers, an upload resume test, a range test, an auth flow test per method, run in its CI.
- The seed script no longer creates fixed users in production (`scripts/seed.js` lines 49 to 75 today).
- The application stays in its own repository and consumes the published pre-release packages, because that exercises the install path users take; it is also linked from the docs as the reference deployment.

Effort: about 30 engineer-days for the rebuild and its tests (judgment; the application is 81 server files and about 100 routes), plus about 10 days spread over steps 9, 16, 19, 22, 24, 25, 26 and 29 for the sixteen framework changes, which are priced there rather than here. R.6's total becomes about 800 days.

Open questions with recommended defaults:

- Which facade? Node, because the frontend and the server rendering are zero-query and the SSR entry point is Node code; a Python or C# port is a separate binding exercise, not part of R.8.
- Does the ZIP streamer move into the core? No; `zero-compress` provides raw DEFLATE and CRC32, and the ZIP64 container stays application code, since no other consumer needs it yet.
- Does R.8 start before release 3? Yes, in two passes: the routing, static, WebSocket, upload and download paths on the 2.0.0-beta line after release 2 (that pass is the first real streaming-ABI consumer and will find its gaps), then auth, ORM, WebRTC and observability on the release 3 line.
